name: Sudhira Das
title: Sudhira Das: From a First to a Place for Others
description: The engineer and educator remembered for helping build opportunities for women’s technical training in Odisha.
author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs.text: Sudhira Das is remembered as Odisha’s first woman engineer. In the memorial her grandson Abhirup Anand wrote when she died in 2015, that distinction leads to another achievement: her part in establishing the Women’s Polytechnic at Bhubaneswar. Her story concerns both entering a technical profession and helping create a place where other women could train for work.

The dates in institutional records give that story a practical shape. S.K.D.A.V. Government Polytechnic in Rourkela places her first in its list of principals, serving from 1 April 1974 to 24 July 1977. It is a clear record of a woman holding responsibility for technical education, beyond the shorthand of a pioneering qualification.

According to Anand’s account, Das was born in Cuttack in 1932, graduated from Ravenshaw College in 1951 and completed an M.Sc.(Tech) in Radio Physics and Electronics in Calcutta in 1956. The following year she joined Berhampur Engineering School as a lecturer in science and mathematics. The movement from studying to teaching matters: the knowledge she had acquired became part of other students’ preparation.
Teaching asks an educator to make a subject understandable; running an institution asks her to give that teaching a dependable home. Das held both responsibilities.

The Bhubaneswar polytechnic’s own history describes a modest beginning. Established in 1978 as Women’s Polytechnic, it initially had one department: Stenography and Secretarial Practice, taught as a two-year course. In 1992 that course became a three-year diploma in Modern Office Management. Practical training for office work stood at the beginning of the institution’s history.

Anand credits his grandmother with establishing this institution. The college history records its opening year and original programme without naming her individual role. His remembrance gives those institutional beginnings a personal connection: a grandmother whose work helped other women prepare for employment.

Das’s legacy invites us to look beyond the word “first”. The opportunities that follow a pioneer depend on classrooms, courses and people willing to take responsibility for them. Remembering her as a teacher and educational leader gives that continuing work a place beside the milestone.
